description: Lunav(Lunar Navigation) develops data-driven solutions to identify safe and optimal landing sites on the Moon. Using open NASA datasets, our team bridges space science and technology to guide the future of lunar exploration.
summary:
**Lunav One** is an interactive lunar exploration platform developed to help users understand how terrain, location, and time influence sunlight and Earth visibility on the Moon, particularly near its south pole. These conditions are important considerations for future lunar surface exploration.

Using NASA data from JPL Horizons, LOLA, and LROC, Lunav One combines an interactive 3D Moon, a south polar map, and a catalog of 17 documented lunar locations. Users can explore environmental conditions over time, visualize sunlight and Earth visibility indicators, and use a Site Planner to evaluate different locations, asset heights, and analysis periods.
By transforming complex scientific data into an accessible and interactive experience, Lunav One makes lunar exploration more approachable for students, educators, and space enthusiasts. It helps users explore the environmental challenges of the Moon while encouraging informed discussions about future missions.
Lunav One is an educational and exploratory tool, not a system for certifying landing safety or operational communications.
details:
Lunav One is an interactive web application developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, designed to make lunar environmental data accessible and understandable. It focuses on how terrain, location, and time influence solar illumination and Earth visibility, particularly near the lunar south pole, where these conditions are important for future exploration.

How does it work?

The application combines an interactive 3D Moon, a detailed south polar map, and a catalog of 17 documented lunar locations. Users can explore NASA imagery, examine scientific information about each location, and visualize modeled sunlight and Earth visibility conditions.

An interactive timeline allows users to observe how these conditions change over time. Sun and Earth indicators update dynamically, while charts and metrics provide additional information about illumination, visibility, and periods of darkness.

The Site Planner allows users to select predefined or custom locations, adjust asset height, define an elevation mask, and choose an analysis period. It also provides a Site Neighborhood visualization, allowing users to investigate how environmental conditions vary across nearby positions.

Technologies and development

Lunav One uses NASA's JPL Horizons ephemerides, LOLA elevation data, and LROC imagery available through NASA Moon Trek. Our calculations combine astronomical information with terrain-aware horizon modeling to estimate solar illumination and geometric Earth visibility.

The application was developed using Python, Streamlit, Pandas, NumPy, Rasterio, Requests, and Plotly. Its interactive lunar visualizations use JavaScript, WebGL, Three.js, globe.gl, and Leaflet.

To improve responsiveness, hourly data for 17 catalog locations were precomputed for 2027–2028, while supported custom scenarios can be calculated dynamically. The application runs in a web browser and does not require specialized hardware.

Creativity and impact

The project's creativity lies in combining scientific calculations, real lunar imagery, and interactive visualization within a single accessible platform. Instead of presenting complex datasets through static tables, Lunav One lets users explore spatial and temporal changes directly on the Moon.

The intended impact is educational: helping students, educators, space enthusiasts, and future researchers better understand the environmental challenges of lunar exploration.

Scientific considerations

Our team considered terrain resolution, coordinate accuracy, data provenance, temporal coverage, computational performance, and scientific transparency.

We compared our results with published references. Solar illumination estimates for four studied locations differed by less than 1.2 percentage points from Gläser et al. (2017), while Earth visibility results for seven locations differed by at most 4.6 percentage points from NASA PGDA reference values.

These comparisons demonstrate consistency with published results, not independent validation, since some underlying terrain data are shared. Lunav One is an educational and exploratory prototype; it does not certify landing safety, electrical power availability, or operational communications.
